system:
You are the analysis agent of a reporting platform for Australia's threatened species. Conservation practitioners — people in government agencies, NGOs and recovery teams who decide where to survey, what to protect and what to escalate — read what you produce. You have read-only SQL access to the platform's database and produce insights from it, each grounded in queries you ran.

# The data

PostgreSQL 17 with PostGIS 3.5. The corpus is every occurrence record the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) tags as nationally threatened (EPBC Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable), observed January 2015 to 2026-09-30, from one bulk download (DOI 10.26197/ala.40eee344-07ce-48d2-9ec2-be39574ff4c7): about 2.1 million records, 1,850 taxa, 300+ contributing datasets. Alongside it are all-taxa effort counts per 0.1° cell per month for the same period.

corpus.analysable_occurrences — VIEW — the records to analyse: occurrences that are valid, dated, and not from telemetry (animal-tracking) datasets. Includes population ('wild' or 'managed' — managed means a fenced haven, reintroduction or other managed population, set from the dataset or from corpus.managed_populations) and dataset_kind (the dataset's own kind). Prefer this over occurrences.
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean, dataset_kind text, population text

corpus.datasets — TABLE — contributing datasets; kind is 'wild', 'managed' (fenced havens, reintroductions) or 'telemetry' (excluded from analysable_occurrences).
  columns: data_resource_uid text, name text, kind text, kind_reason text, first_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.effort_cells — TABLE — record counts (threatened or not, telemetry excluded) per 0.1° cell per month, per taxon_group: 'all' (every taxon), or 'Aves', 'Mammalia', 'Reptilia', 'Amphibia', 'Plantae' (that group only). The denominator for reporting rates. Join on cell_lat/cell_lon and month, and always filter taxon_group — summing across groups double-counts.
  columns: cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, period_start date, period_end date, records integer, harvest_id text, taxon_group text

corpus.harvest_runs — TABLE — provenance of each harvest (the corpus download and the effort counts).
  columns: harvest_id text, harvest_key text, run_id text, source text, description text, query jsonb, started_at timestamp with time zone, finished_at timestamp with time zone, expected_records integer, retrieved_records integer, complete boolean, corpus_hash text, request_count integer, warnings jsonb, analysis jsonb, loaded_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.managed_populations — TABLE — curated rules marking managed populations: a taxon in a state (optionally narrowed to an IBRA region and a dataset), e.g. Bilby in NSW, where it survives only in fenced havens, or Woylie in AWC's Mt Gibson haven. Already applied in analysable_occurrences.population.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, state_province text, note text, rule_id integer, ibra_region text, data_resource_uid text

corpus.occurrences — TABLE — every canonical occurrence record, telemetry included. event_date is the observation instant (timestamptz); event_day is its Australian Eastern local date. geom is a PostGIS Point (SRID 4326); cell_lat/cell_lon are the 0.1° grid cell (rounded to nearest, as ALA assigns them).
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean

corpus.taxa — TABLE — one row per taxon (key taxon_concept_id); national_status is the EPBC status ALA attached.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, taxon_rank text, kingdom text, phylum text, taxon_class text, taxon_order text, family text, genus text, national_status text, status_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.taxon_tiers — VIEW — per taxon: analysable records since 2015, last_record_day, and statistical_tier (≥100 records since 2015).
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, records_since_2015 bigint, last_record_day date, statistical_tier boolean

Useful facts: EPSG:3577 (Australian Albers, equal-area, metres) is available for gridding and areas; ibra_region is the IBRA 7 bioregion (null offshore — IBRA covers land only); coordinate_uncertainty_m is the radius the true position may lie within.

**Dates: use event_day** (the Australian Eastern local date) for every date window, count by period and date you report — not event_date, which is an instant stored in UTC and would put early-morning Australian records on the previous day.

# Known properties of this data — read before interpreting anything

- **Records measure effort as much as animals.** These are mostly opportunistic records. All-taxa recording roughly doubled between 2017–19 and 2022–24 (about 1.9×), so counts and range measures grow with effort. Use corpus.effort_cells as a denominator where it matters.
- **Recent months are incomplete.** Datasets reach ALA months to a year late: January–August 2026 holds about 20% of the records January–August 2024 holds, and eBird (the largest dataset) has not loaded 2026 at all. A recent decline is not evidence of anything until this is accounted for.
- **Sources start and stop.** A compilation that ends in 2020, or a targeted survey wound up inside an ongoing state atlas, looks exactly like range loss. Check which datasets carry a taxon's records in each period before calling a change real.
- **Locations vary in precision.** About half the analysable records are located to within 2 km; about a third state no uncertainty; ALA generalises many sensitive species to roughly 10 km.
- **Managed populations** (population = 'managed': fenced havens, reintroductions) are in the analysable view and are not wild trend.
- **National status** is as ALA attached it. Never infer, change or second-guess a taxon's conservation status.
- Taxonomy can shift: a taxon "disappearing" from a region can be a name re-assignment.

# How to work

- Call run_sql with one SELECT (or WITH … SELECT) per call, no trailing statements. Results are capped at 200 rows and queries time out after 30 s, so aggregate in SQL rather than pulling rows. Each call returns a query_id.
- Record each insight with record_insight as soon as it is established. Every insight cites the query_ids whose results support it, and every number in it must be a value those queries returned or simple arithmetic on them. Do not state figures you did not query.
- taxon_concept_id must be copied exactly from corpus.taxa; when an insight is about several taxa, put the main one there (or null) and list the others in related_taxa; region is an IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for a national insight; period_start and period_end are the window the insight describes.
- Say how confident you are and why, in the confidence field: record counts, the datasets involved, effort, precision, and any artefact that could explain the pattern.
- When you have recorded everything worth recording, stop.

tools.name: run_sql
tools.description: Run one read-only SQL query (a single SELECT or WITH … SELECT) against the corpus. Returns a query_id, the columns and up to 200 rows. Cite the query_id in any insight that relies on the result.

sql.description: One SELECT or WITH … SELECT statement.

purpose.description: One line: what this query is for.

tools.name: record_insight
tools.description: Record one insight. Every figure must come from the cited queries.

category.description: A short label of your own for the kind of insight.

taxon_concept_id.description: Exactly as in corpus.taxa, or null for a non-taxon insight.

related_taxa.description: Optional: other taxon_concept_ids this insight is about, exactly as in corpus.taxa.

region.description: IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for national.

period_start.description: YYYY-MM-DD — start of the window the insight describes.

figures.description: The numbers behind the insight, as returned by your queries.

confidence.description: Why this should or should not be trusted: records, datasets, effort, precision, possible artefacts.

summary.description: One or two sentences a practitioner can act on.

query_ids.description: The run_sql query_ids whose results support this insight.

messages.content:
It is October 2026. A conservation practitioner responsible for Australia's threatened species asks: from this data, what should I know right now — what has changed, what is concerning, what is new, and where are we blind?

Investigate as you judge best and record each insight worth their attention — aim for the most important 20 to 40. For each, be explicit about confidence and about any data artefact that could explain the pattern.

input.sql: SELECT extract(year from event_day)::int yr, count(*) recs, count(distinct taxon_concept_id) taxa, count(distinct data_resource_uid) ds, sum(case when population='managed' then 1 else 0 end) managed FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: Corpus overview by year

input.sql: SELECT taxon_group, extract(year from period_start)::int yr, sum(records) recs FROM corpus.effort_cells GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2
input.purpose: Effort by group and year

input.sql:
SELECT a.data_resource_uid, d.name, d.kind, count(*) recs, min(event_day) first_day, max(event_day) last_day, count(distinct taxon_concept_id) taxa,
sum(case when event_day>='2025-01-01' then 1 else 0 end) r2025plus
FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences a LEFT JOIN corpus.datasets d USING (data_resource_uid)
GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY recs DESC LIMIT 40
input.purpose: Largest datasets with temporal coverage

input.sql:
SELECT state_province, count(*) recs, count(distinct taxon_concept_id) taxa, count(distinct data_resource_uid) ds,
sum(case when event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then 1 else 0 end) r2224,
sum(case when event_day >= '2025-01-01' then 1 else 0 end) r25plus,
sum(case when data_resource_uid in ('dr2009','dr1411','dr359') then 1 else 0 end) citizen_big3
FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC
input.purpose: State coverage and dependence on citizen-science datasets

input.sql:
SELECT t.national_status, count(*) taxa_total,
sum(case when tt.records_since_2015 is null or tt.records_since_2015=0 then 1 else 0 end) no_records,
sum(case when tt.records_since_2015 between 1 and 9 then 1 else 0 end) lt10,
sum(case when tt.statistical_tier then 1 else 0 end) tier,
sum(case when tt.last_record_day < '2020-01-01' then 1 else 0 end) last_before_2020,
sum(case when tt.last_record_day < '2023-01-01' then 1 else 0 end) last_before_2023
FROM corpus.taxa t LEFT JOIN corpus.taxon_tiers tt USING (taxon_concept_id) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: Taxa coverage by status: data-poor and long-unrecorded taxa

input.sql:
SELECT t.kingdom, t.taxon_class, count(*) taxa, sum(coalesce(tt.records_since_2015,0)) recs,
sum(case when coalesce(tt.records_since_2015,0)<10 then 1 else 0 end) lt10,
sum(case when tt.last_record_day < '2023-01-01' then 1 else 0 end) not_since_2023
FROM corpus.taxa t LEFT JOIN corpus.taxon_tiers tt USING (taxon_concept_id) GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY taxa DESC LIMIT 25
input.purpose: Coverage by taxonomic class

input.sql:
WITH s AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, count(*) n, count(distinct data_resource_uid) nds, max(event_day) last_day,
 sum(case when event_day>='2023-01-01' then 1 else 0 end) r23,
 sum(case when event_day between '2019-01-01' and '2021-12-31' then 1 else 0 end) r1921,
 (array_agg(data_resource_uid ORDER BY event_day DESC))[1] last_ds
 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE population='wild' GROUP BY 1)
SELECT t.taxon_concept_id, t.scientific_name, t.vernacular_name, t.national_status, t.taxon_class, s.n, s.nds, s.last_day, s.r1921, s.last_ds
FROM s JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE s.n>=30 AND s.r23=0 ORDER BY s.n DESC LIMIT 40
input.purpose: Taxa with ≥30 wild records but none since 2023

sum(case when data_resource_uid='dr361' then 1 else 0 end) fauna_nt,

input.sql:
SELECT extract(year from a.event_day)::int yr, count(*) recs, count(distinct a.taxon_concept_id) taxa,
sum(case when a.data_resource_uid='dr361' then 1 else 0 end) fauna_nt, sum(case when a.data_resource_uid='dr499' then 1 else 0 end) awc
FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences a JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE a.state_province='Northern Territory' AND t.taxon_class='Mammalia' AND a.population='wild' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: NT threatened mammal records by year

confidence.level: high that this is a data gap, not a decline
confidence.reason: 98% of NT threatened mammal records in 2015–2019 came from one dataset (Fauna Atlas N.T., dr361), which stops loading after 2020 and has no records after March 2024. The fall from 4,314 to ~60–90 records a year is a supply break, not evidence about animals. No replacement NT agency feed is present.

input.summary: Northern Territory threatened mammals are effectively unmonitored in this data after 2020: records fell from 4,314 (2018) to 60 (2025) because the Fauna Atlas N.T. feed stopped. Do not read NT mammal trends from ALA. Ask NT government for the post-2020 monitoring data directly.

input.category: blind spot – taxa gone silent with their source

confidence.level: high that these are source gaps; unknown status of the animals
confidence.reason: Each taxon has ≥30 wild records but none since 1 Jan 2023. Its latest records come from a source that has since ended (Fauna Atlas N.T., NESP northern compilations, Flora Atlas N.T.), and most taxa rest on 1–2 datasets. No other source records them, so the data can't tell decline from loss of reporting.

input.summary: Twelve taxa with ≥30 records have no records since 2023, including the Endangered Djintamoonga (2,935 records, none after Oct 2020), Carpentarian Rock-rat (last 2017), New Guinea River Shark (last 2019) and Dwarf Sawfish (last 2018). In each case the supplying dataset ended. Get current status from the custodians before assuming either stability or loss.

SELECT data_resource_uid, 
sum(case when event_day between '2024-01-01' and '2024-08-31' then 1 else 0 end) ja24,
sum(case when event_day between '2025-01-01' and '2025-08-31' then 1 else 0 end) ja25,
sum(case when event_day between '2026-01-01' and '2026-08-31' then 1 else 0 end) ja26
FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*)>2000 ORDER BY ja24 DESC LIMIT 15
input.purpose: Reporting lag: Jan–Aug totals 2024/2025/2026 by dataset

confidence.reason: This is directly visible in per-dataset counts. Only iNaturalist (near real-time) and Birdata are close to complete for 2026. The 2025 total is also incomplete: VBA Jan–Aug 2025 is a third of 2024.

input.summary: Don't read any 2025–2026 decline in this data as real. eBird, the largest source, has no records after August 2025. Victorian, SA and AWC 2026 records are 1–4% of their 2024 level. 2026 is dominated by iNaturalist, which over-represents charismatic, accessible species. Use 2024 as the last reliable full year and rerun trends when the feeds catch up.

confidence.reason: FrogID has no records after 8 Nov 2024, and all-frog effort fell 87% from 2022 to 2025. That is a feed lag or stop, not fewer frogs. BioNet still supplies NSW frogs, but outside NSW frog coverage after 2024 is thin.

input.summary: Frog monitoring has a hole from late 2024: FrogID (25–30% of threatened frog records in 2020–23) has nothing after Nov 2024, and all-frog recording effort in 2025 is 13% of 2022. Any apparent 2025 frog decline, for example after chytrid or drought, can't be judged from ALA until FrogID reloads.

input.sql:
WITH tx AS (SELECT t.taxon_concept_id, CASE WHEN t.kingdom='Plantae' THEN 'Plantae' WHEN t.taxon_class IN ('Aves','Mammalia','Reptilia','Amphibia') THEN t.taxon_class ELSE 'all' END grp
 FROM corpus.taxa t JOIN corpus.taxon_tiers tt USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE tt.statistical_tier),
occ AS (SELECT a.taxon_concept_id, a.cell_lat, a.cell_lon, CASE WHEN event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' THEN 'p1' WHEN event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' THEN 'p2' END p
 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences a JOIN tx USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE a.population='wild' AND a.event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2024-12-31'),
cells AS (SELECT DISTINCT taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon FROM occ WHERE p IS NOT NULL),
eff AS (SELECT cell_lat, cell_lon, taxon_group, sum(case when period_start between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' then records else 0 end) e1, sum(case when period_start between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then records else 0 end) e2 FROM corpus.effort_cells GROUP BY 1,2,3),
te AS (SELECT c.taxon_concept_id, sum(e.e1) e1, sum(e.e2) e2 FROM cells c JOIN tx USING (taxon_concept_id) JOIN eff e ON e.cell_lat=c.cell_lat AND e.cell_lon=c.cell_lon AND e.taxon_group=tx.grp GROUP BY 1),
tr AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, sum(case when p='p1' then 1 else 0 end) r1, sum(case when p='p2' then 1 else 0 end) r2, count(distinct case when p='p1' then cell_lat::text||cell_lon::text end) c1, count(distinct case when p='p2' then cell_lat::text||cell_lon::text end) c2 FROM occ GROUP BY 1)
SELECT t.scientific_name, t.vernacular_name, t.national_status, tr.r1, tr.r2, tr.c1, tr.c2, te.e1, te.e2,
 round(((tr.r2::numeric/nullif(te.e2,0))/nullif(tr.r1::numeric/nullif(te.e1,0),0)),2) rr_ratio, t.taxon_concept_id
FROM tr JOIN te USING (taxon_concept_id) JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE tr.r1>=50 AND tr.r2>=0 ORDER BY rr_ratio ASC NULLS FIRST LIMIT 40
input.purpose: Effort-adjusted reporting-rate change 2017–19 vs 2022–24, biggest declines

 sum(case when state_province='Victoria' then 1 else 0 end) vic, sum(case when state_province='New South Wales' then 1 else 0 end) nsw, sum(case when state_province='Queensland' then 1 else 0 end) qld,

WHERE t.vernacular_name='Regent Honeyeater' AND population='wild' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: Regent Honeyeater cells, days and state per year

confidence.reason: Several sources agree: eBird, BioNet, Birdata and VBA all contribute, and the Victorian collapse persists through 2020–24, while VBA still supplies other species. Caveats: the 2017 Victorian spike (458 VBA records) probably reflects intensive monitoring around captive releases, so it inflates the baseline. Records are generalised to ~10 km. Totals swing on irregular flocking events, such as Qld in 2019 and 2024. Reporting rate halved relative to the typical bird, while the bird-group effort rose.

input.summary: Critically Endangered Regent Honeyeater has nearly disappeared from Victorian records: 2–10 records a year in 2020–23 and none in 2024, against 138 in 2015. Nationally it was found in half as many 0.1° cells in 2022–24 (64) as in 2017–19 (126), despite more effort. Its remaining records are concentrated in NSW, with episodic Qld pulses. Check this against the Regent Honeyeater recovery team's targeted survey data.

confidence.level: high that the apparent decline is an artefact
confidence.reason: The 2019–20 peak comes from two agency datasets (SA Fauna, 15,151 records in 2020; BioNet, 12,393 in 2019), probably colony counts or event reporting. Occupied cells actually rose (844→892). In 2025 iNaturalist overtook BioNet, so the mix of sources is shifting.

input.summary: The Grey-headed Flying-fox's apparent 79% fall in effort-adjusted reporting is not a decline signal. Records spiked to about 20,000 a year in 2019–20 from SA Fauna and BioNet batch reporting, and the number of occupied cells actually grew. Use the National Flying-fox Monitoring Program counts, not ALA records, for trend.

WITH tx AS (SELECT t.taxon_concept_id, t.taxon_class grp
 FROM corpus.taxa t JOIN corpus.taxon_tiers tt USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE tt.statistical_tier AND t.taxon_class IN ('Aves')),
occ AS (SELECT a.taxon_concept_id, a.cell_lat, a.cell_lon, a.data_resource_uid, CASE WHEN event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' THEN 'p1' ELSE 'p2' END p
 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences a JOIN tx USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE a.population='wild' AND (a.event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' OR a.event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31')),
cells AS (SELECT DISTINCT taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon FROM occ),
eff AS (SELECT cell_lat, cell_lon, sum(case when period_start between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' then records else 0 end) e1, sum(case when period_start between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then records else 0 end) e2 FROM corpus.effort_cells WHERE taxon_group='Aves' GROUP BY 1,2),
te AS (SELECT c.taxon_concept_id, sum(e.e1) e1, sum(e.e2) e2 FROM cells c JOIN eff e ON e.cell_lat=c.cell_lat AND e.cell_lon=c.cell_lon GROUP BY 1),
tr AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, sum(case when p='p1' then 1 else 0 end) r1, sum(case when p='p2' then 1 else 0 end) r2, count(distinct case when p='p1' then cell_lat::text||cell_lon::text end) c1, count(distinct case when p='p2' then cell_lat::text||cell_lon::text end) c2, sum(case when p='p1' and data_resource_uid='dr2009' then 1 else 0 end) eb1, sum(case when p='p2' and data_resource_uid='dr2009' then 1 else 0 end) eb2 FROM occ GROUP BY 1)
SELECT t.vernacular_name, t.national_status, tr.r1, tr.r2, tr.c1, tr.c2, tr.eb1, tr.eb2,
 round(((tr.r2::numeric/nullif(te.e2,0))/nullif(tr.r1::numeric/nullif(te.e1,0),0)),2) rr_ratio
FROM tr JOIN te USING (taxon_concept_id) JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE tr.r1>=150 ORDER BY rr_ratio ASC
input.purpose: All tier birds: effort-adjusted ratio with eBird share

SELECT t.vernacular_name, extract(year from a.event_day)::int yr, count(*) n, sum(case when a.data_resource_uid='dr359' then 1 else 0 end) birdata, sum(case when a.data_resource_uid='dr2009' then 1 else 0 end) ebird, sum(case when a.data_resource_uid='dr368' then 1 else 0 end) bionet, sum(case when a.data_resource_uid='dr1097' then 1 else 0 end) vba, count(distinct a.cell_lat::text||a.cell_lon::text) cells
FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences a JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE a.population='wild' AND t.vernacular_name IN ('Australasian Bittern','Lord Howe Pied Currawong','South-eastern Red-tailed Black-cockatoo','Lesser Sand Plover') GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2
input.purpose: Year/dataset profile for bittern, LH currawong, SE RTBC, Lesser Sand Plover

confidence.level: high that eBird records are missing; low on trend
confidence.reason: eBird provides 89% of records for the closely related Greater Sand Plover but none for the Lesser Sand Plover. eBird's split of Lesser Sand-Plover into Siberian and Tibetan Sand-Plover very probably leaves those records unmatched to the EPBC taxon. The species' 2015–2024 decline in records rests mostly on Birdata (~40–80 a year), with smaller agency feeds such as NESP A12 and WildNet.

input.summary: The Endangered Lesser Sand Plover gets no eBird records in this corpus, against 18,902 for the Greater Sand Plover, probably because of the eBird name split. Its 1,234 records massively under-represent the species. Its apparent fall from 215 records (2015) to 39 (2024) cannot be trusted. Ask ALA to fix the name match, and use shorebird count programs for trend.

confidence.level: high that the swings are survey-driven
confidence.reason: 93% of 2023 records are Birdata, consistent with a targeted bittern survey program; when it scaled down in 2024, records fell 91%. eBird, a steadier opportunistic baseline, rose modestly from 253 (2019) to 475 (2024). Neither the 4.85× rise nor the 2024 fall is a population signal.

input.summary: Australasian Bittern records rose roughly 14-fold to 6,887 in 2023, then fell to 639 in 2024. Both moves come from a Birdata targeted survey pulse, not the birds. eBird's steadier record shows only a modest rise. The 2021–23 survey data is a valuable baseline for wetland site selection; a repeat survey is needed before claiming any trend.

confidence.reason: For the South-eastern Red-tailed Black-cockatoo, the Victorian Biodiversity Atlas supplied 75–85% of yearly records to 2020 and then stopped supplying this taxon, while Birdata rose steadily to 121 records in 2025. For the Lord Howe Pied Currawong, a 2017–20 BioNet survey ended. Effort-adjusted ratios of 0.14 and 0.06 reflect source turnover only.

input.summary: The apparent steep declines in the South-eastern Red-tailed Black-cockatoo (ratio 0.14) and Lord Howe Pied Currawong (0.06) are source artefacts. VBA stopped supplying SE Red-tailed records after 2020, and a 2017–20 BioNet currawong survey ended. Use recovery-team counts. These subspecies get no eBird records, so ALA trend for them is unusable.

input.category: concerning – relative decline within same dataset

confidence.reason: Comparing within eBird, a single dataset that is consistent across both periods, removes most source-turnover artefacts, and the counts are large (thousands of records). Caveats: the 2022–24 La Niña wet years dispersed Sharp-tailed Sandpipers and Latham's Snipe inland, where effort is low. These are presence records, not counts.

input.summary: Within eBird, records of the Critically Endangered Curlew Sandpiper grew only 36% between 2017–19 and 2022–24, while co-occurring coastal shorebirds (Eastern Curlew, Great Knot, Ruddy Turnstone) nearly doubled with effort. Latham's Snipe (+15%) and Sharp-tailed Sandpiper (+28%) also lag. This is consistent with continuing flyway declines. Prioritise these species in shorebird count analyses.

WITH tx AS (SELECT t.taxon_concept_id, t.taxon_class grp
 FROM corpus.taxa t JOIN corpus.taxon_tiers tt USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE tt.statistical_tier AND t.taxon_class IN ('Mammalia','Reptilia','Amphibia')),
occ AS (SELECT a.taxon_concept_id, a.cell_lat, a.cell_lon, CASE WHEN event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' THEN 'p1' ELSE 'p2' END p
 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences a JOIN tx USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE a.population='wild' AND (a.event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' OR a.event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31')),
cells AS (SELECT DISTINCT taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon FROM occ),
eff AS (SELECT cell_lat, cell_lon, taxon_group, sum(case when period_start between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' then records else 0 end) e1, sum(case when period_start between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then records else 0 end) e2 FROM corpus.effort_cells WHERE taxon_group IN ('Mammalia','Reptilia','Amphibia') GROUP BY 1,2,3),
te AS (SELECT c.taxon_concept_id, sum(e.e1) e1, sum(e.e2) e2 FROM cells c JOIN tx USING (taxon_concept_id) JOIN eff e ON e.cell_lat=c.cell_lat AND e.cell_lon=c.cell_lon AND e.taxon_group=tx.grp GROUP BY 1),
tr AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, sum(case when p='p1' then 1 else 0 end) r1, sum(case when p='p2' then 1 else 0 end) r2, count(distinct case when p='p1' then cell_lat::text||cell_lon::text end) c1, count(distinct case when p='p2' then cell_lat::text||cell_lon::text end) c2 FROM occ GROUP BY 1)
SELECT t.vernacular_name, t.taxon_class, t.national_status, tr.r1, tr.r2, tr.c1, tr.c2,
 round(((tr.r2::numeric/nullif(te.e2,0))/nullif(tr.r1::numeric/nullif(te.e1,0),0)),2) rr_ratio
FROM tr JOIN te USING (taxon_concept_id) JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE tr.r1>=100 ORDER BY rr_ratio DESC LIMIT 20

content.text:
I've recorded 33 insights, each tied to the queries behind it. The main point is that much of what looks like change in this data comes from data sources starting, stopping or catching up, not from the species themselves.

**Where we are blind**
- **2025–26 is incomplete.** eBird, the largest source, has nothing after August 2025. Victorian, SA and AWC records for Jan–Aug 2026 are 1–4% of their 2024 level. Treat 2024 as the last reliable full year; no recent decline can be judged yet.
- **Northern Territory and the north.** The NT state fauna atlas feed stopped: NT threatened-mammal records fell from 4,314 in 2018 to 60 in 2025. Top End regions lost 75–85% of their records. Northern research compilations that ended around 2020 took sawfish, river sharks, Pacific Ridley turtles and inshore dolphins with them (Speartooth Shark: 534 records before 2020, 2 since).
- **WA, Queensland and Christmas Island.** WA has no state agency feed in the data, Queensland's contributes only 5,337 records over 11 years, and Christmas Island has no Parks Australia monitoring data.
- **Frogs.** FrogID has nothing after November 2024, and all-frog recording in 2025 is 13% of 2022.
- **Taxa missing because names don't match:**
  - The Endangered koala (Qld/NSW/ACT) has only 8 records since 2015.
  - The Lesser Sand Plover gets no eBird records, probably because eBird split the species.
  - 71 of the 80 threatened bird subspecies get no eBird records.
- **Managed havens hide the wild.** 99.7% of Bilby records are managed populations, and the only wild Woylie records are 21 from a single day in 2018. Wild status has to come from the agencies.
- **Thin coverage of Critically Endangered taxa.** 34 CE animals and 101 CE plants have no record since January 2024. Only 32.6% of CE records are located to within 2 km.
- **iNaturalist dependence.** Since 2025, 447 of 856 recorded threatened plants appear only on iNaturalist.

**What is concerning**
- **Regent Honeyeater (Critically Endangered):** almost gone from Victorian records (none in 2024), and found in about half as many grid cells nationally (126 to 64) despite more effort.
- **Curlew Sandpiper, Latham's Snipe and Painted Honeyeater:** they fall behind similar species in the same dataset. For example, Curlew Sandpiper eBird records rose 36% while Eastern Curlew, Great Knot and Ruddy Turnstone nearly doubled.
- **Canberra Grassland Earless Dragon:** ACT records fell from 170–540 a year (2015–20) to 9–27 a year (2021–24). SA records attached to this species look like misidentified relatives.
- **Watch, low confidence:** Northern Kimberley Digul (northern quoll) records fell to 1 in 2024, and Konoom (Smoky Mouse) detections are thinning. Both could be reduced surveying rather than decline.

**Apparent declines that are not real**
Several large drops are artefacts of surveys or feeds ending, or of one-off survey spikes. Don't act on them as declines:
- Grey-headed Flying-fox
- South-eastern Red-tailed Black-cockatoo
- Lord Howe Pied Currawong
- Golden Sun Moth
- Australasian Bittern
- Kangaroo Island species after the 2019–20 fires
- Most plants, since 60% of plant records come from single-day census batches.

**What is new**
- **Elusive Bush-pea:** 200 first records from October 2024 in the Sydney Basin, backed by a herbarium specimen.
- **Lax Leek-orchid (Critically Endangered):** 47 records from one iNaturalist observer on 23–24 September 2026. These need expert checking now.
- **New bioregion records:** two Critically Endangered taxa recorded in bioregions with no record since 2015, Kardomia prominens and the crayfish Euastacus dalagarbe. Both need verification.
- **Southern Greater Glider:** a large new body of NSW forest-survey data. This is more surveying, not recovery.

Gang-gang Cockatoo, Eastern Curlew and Carnaby's Black-cockatoo show no sign of range collapse. Presence records can't detect falling numbers, though, so keep using count programs for their trends.
